odeProperty.value: We continue our journey through the Renaissance.

odeComponent.htmlView:
The Renaissance was a cultural and artistic movement of the 15th and 16th centuries that marked the beginning of the Modern Age in Europe.

  • A changing society (the bourgeoisie): wealthy merchants and bankers in the cities gained enormous economic power. They used their money to become patrons, funding artists to gain prestige, whilst the feudal nobility lost its former influence.
  • Monarchies and Capitalism (Politics and Economy): kings concentrated power by establishing authoritarian monarchies (the origin of the modern state). At the same time, the medieval agrarian economy gave way to a commercial form of capitalism based on banking, currency and maritime trade with the Americas.
  • Crisis and Anthropocentrism (Religion): the mindset shifted towards anthropocentrism (the human being as the centre of everything, using reason and science). Furthermore, the Church was fractured by Martin Luther’s Protestant Reformation, which divided Europe along religious lines.
  • The Information Revolution (The Printing Press): Gutenberg’s invention enabled the mass reproduction of books, making culture more affordable. It was the key tool that allowed the ideas of scientists, humanists and religious reformers to spread rapidly across the continent.

During the Renaissance, music underwent major changes, particularly in the field of vocal music. The Renaissance was the era of polyphony, or multi-voice composition, which definitively supplanted medieval monody.


What are we going to learn?

    2.2 – Secular vocal music

odeNavStructureProperty.value: 1.1. Música monofónica religiosa: el canto gregoriano.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Religious music took on an international character. The most prominent composers were appointed as chapel masters at the major cathedrals and travelled constantly throughout Europe.

  • The main genre of religious music was the motet, a piece for several voices (usually four or five), based on a religious text in Latin and with a predominantly polyphonic texture, which employed the technique of imitative counterpoint.
  • The other religious musical genre is the Mass. It was composed by setting the most important prayers of this service to music, namely the Kyrie eleison (Lord, have mercy), Gloria, Credo, Sanctus and the Agnus Dei (Lamb of God).

Some notable composers included Josquin des Prez, Orlando di Lasso and Giovanni Perluigi da Palestrina. In Spain, Tomás Luis de Victoria (Ávila) and Cristóbal de Morales and Francisco Guerrero, both from Seville, stood out.

odeNavStructureProperty.value: 1.2. Música monofónica profana: trovadores y troveros

odeComponent.htmlView:
As Renaissance sacred music was acquiring its "international" style, secular music also began to diversify, developing discrete styles that reflected individual countries or regions. During this era, the two dominant types of music were the madrigal in Italy and the chanson in France:

Chanson Lyrics in French, simple melodies, sung for the general public; used four or five voices and were written about various themes (love, satire, etc.).
Madrigal Poetic lyrics in Italian; used four or five voices and were written mostly about love.

odeComponent.htmlView:
As you know, the madrigal originated in Italy and the chanson in France. This time, you’ll embark on a musical journey through two other regions – Spain and England – to discover new genres.

Villancico Lyrics in Spanish. A villancico consisted of two alternating parts, called the refrain (estribillo) and stanza (copla). It generally had a romantic or picaresque theme. This has no connection with Spanish Christmas carols
Fa-la-las In England, songs containing musical parts developed on the syllables fa–la–la were popular. They became known as fa–la–la songs, as a result.


Stanza it's like "copla" or "estrofa". Refrain it's the same as chorus or "estribillo".


Religious Christmas carols came into being when the Catholic Church adopted the people’s secular folk songs and changed the lyrics to spread the Christian message. 


In the case of the Fa-la-las, we have a new textural element: homophony. This occurs when all the voices or instruments move together at the same tempo, but sing or play different notes to form chords. In the following audio clips, you will be able to identify which parts are polyphonic and which are homophonic.

odeNavStructureProperty.value: 1.3. Cantigas de Alfonso X el Sabio

odeComponent.htmlView:
During the Renaissance, the profile of instrumental music was much lower than that of vocal music; indeed, its role was relegated to providing a background to songs and dances. However, the situation changed in the sixteenth century, when instrumental music began to be written as compositions in their own right. At first, instrumental music drew on vocal genres such as the motet or the Chanson, adopting different names in the process: ricercare, canzona, etc. However, it wasn’t until the Baroque period that instrumental music came to be regarded as a completely separate entity.

Factors that influenced the development of instrumental music include:

  • Advances in the manufacture of instruments.
  • The more rapid publication of theoretical and practical treatises about instrumental music, enabled by the introduction of the printing press.
  • New systems of notation that did not require extensive musical knowledge (tablature).

Another significant change that influenced instrumental music composition was the use of variations (called diferencias in Spanish). The instrumentalist would overlay a given framework with variations on the original melody. An example of this is in the famous variations of Guárdame las vacas, by Luis de Narváez 

Luis de Narváez - Guárdame las vacas

Dance music was also very important during this period. It became the practice to have dances in pairs, the first dance being slow and the second one fast. This gave rise to common dance pairs such as the Pavane and the Galliard, or the Passamezzo and the Saltarello.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Leading instruments by country

  • Spain: the vihuela (an ancestor of the guitar) was particularly prominent, with famous composers such as Luys de Milán and Narváez.
  • England: ensembles of viola and the virginal (a keyboard instrument) were particularly popular.

The most popular instrument

The lute was the most widespread plucked string instrument throughout Europe. Its most important composer was the Englishman John Dowland.

Evolution into the Baroque period

With the emergence of the modern orchestra during the Baroque period, many Renaissance instruments disappeared. Others evolved to improve their sound:

  • The sackbut evolved into the trombone.
  • The shawm evolved into the oboe.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Religious vocal music (International)

  • Motet: a piece for several voices (usually 4 or 5), based on a religious text in Latin and with a predominantly polyphonic texture, which employs the technique of imitative counterpoint.
  • Mass: polyphonic music in Latin set to the most important prayers of this celebration.

Secular vocal music (National)

  • Chanson: texts in French, with melodic simplicity appealing to the common people, for four or five voices; varied themes (love, satire, etc.).
  • Madrigal: poetic texts in Italian, for four or five voices; usually on the theme of love.
  • Villancico: texts in Spanish. It was based on the alternation of two parts, known as the ‘estribillo’ and the ‘copla’, whose themes were usually romantic or picaresque.
  • Falas: texts in English. They contained musical sections based on the syllables fa-la-la

Instrumental music

  • Variations: based on a given pattern, the instrumentalist would successively vary the original melody.
  • Pavane: slow instrumental dance music, usually in duple metre.
  • Gallarda: fast instrumental dance music, usually in triple metre.
